The holiday season has arrived, and with it, plenty of reasons your fitness routine may slide. Between shopping for gifts, attending holiday parties, and meeting work obligations, it can feel like there’s not enough time to squeeze in an hour-long workout session—so why even try?
Well, consider this: You don’t have to do as much as you think to maintain your fitness between now and New Year’s Day. A review published in the Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research in 2021 suggests that you can reduce your workout time by two-thirds and still maintain your gains, as long as the intensity stays the same.
Researchers also found that, in generally active adults, cutting training frequency to just twice a week for up to 15 weeks could maintain short-term endurance and VO₂ max.
Setting an attainable goal for yourself, like running for at least 30 minutes two or three times per week, can make staying active through the holidays feel more doable. It’s how I was able to get back to exercise after a break, and it’s also how I plan to maintain my fitness this winter—in addition to following some of the best advice from my Runner’s World colleagues.
So ditch the all-or-nothing mindset and use the following tips to your advantage now, so when the New Year arrives, you’ll be ready to tackle your goals for 2027.
6 Tips for Maintaining Fitness During the Busy Holiday Season
1. Spice Up Your Usual Training Plan
“I have a race in mid-January, so I am following a training plan [which keeps me motivated]. But I am also cross-training with step aerobics, and I’ve added jump training into my workouts. I was bored with my usual strength routine, so I decided to mix things up with kettlebell training, targeting my upper body and core.” —Donna Raskin, senior health and fitness editor
“I make time for new workout classes, like the ones offered by Solidcore and OrangeTheory to support my strength needs, because I usually don’t get to attend those sessions when I’m training for a race.” —Sara Hemstock, senior director of marketing and brand liaison
“I love doing strength work and some form of speed training in the winter. I recently found an indoor track in my local YMCA, and I’m excited to use that as an option for when it snows. There’s something nostalgic about it for me after running winter track as a kid.” —Kristine Kearns, associate health and fitness editor
2. Turn a Run Into a Holiday Tradition
“I love running on Christmas Day because it’s always so quiet in my hometown of Columbia, South Carolina. I usually run downtown, past the state capitol building, and through the University of South Carolina. The normally busy area turns into a complete ghost town! It’s a once-a-year experience and a personal tradition. I look forward to it every year.” —Theo Khaler, news editor
3. Sign Up for a Local Race
“Every year, I look forward to going home to North Carolina during the holidays because I get to test my fitness in my neighborhood Turkey Trot. It’s a community event put on by my high school, and it always draws a huge crowd.
The 5K race itself gives me something to look toward and train for in the fall. It’s a great chance to test my speed and have fun with the sport, but the best part has to be the community aspect. I catch up with old friends, teammates, coaches, teachers, and neighbors, and hearing about their own running journeys always fuels mine, too. Plus, each age-group winner wins a pie. Who doesn’t like free dessert?” —Ashley Tysiac, content hype

Holding a stock through 2030 means keeping it for more than four years. A lot can go wrong with any one business in that time, so I'd rather not count on a single company for that long.
My three favorites today are Micron Technology (MU -2.52%), Amazon (AMZN -0.29%), and International Business Machines (IBM +1.00%). They don't look like much of a group. Micron stock trades at under 5 times the earnings analysts expect for this fiscal year, while Amazon trades at around 25 times earnings, using analysts' 2027 forecasts. And IBM's dividend yields about 2.8%.
But I think these differences are a big reason the three fit well together.
Image source: Micron.
1. Micron: The stock looks cheap for what it earns
Micron's growth in the last year has been stunning. Revenue more than tripled in fiscal 2026 to $133.2 billion (Micron's fiscal year ended Sept. 3, 2026), and net income climbed around tenfold to $85.0 billion.
The company's still growing, too. Revenue climbed to $54.2 billion in fiscal Q4 from $41.5 billion the quarter before, and management expects about $61.5 billion in the current one -- slower sequential growth, but growth all the same.
Yet at roughly $820 as of this writing, shares cost under 5 times earnings, using analysts' forecasts for fiscal 2027. In other words, investors are arguably pricing in a steep fall in profits at some point.
There's history behind this doubt. In fiscal 2023, Micron's revenue was around half the prior year's, and the company lost $5.8 billion.
MU Micron Technology
NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/13/26
What makes me comfortable holding through 2030 is how much of the business is now under contract. Micron estimates that its 26 strategic customer agreements will make up over a third of its revenue through 2030. And most of that revenue comes with set pricing terms, often including floor and ceiling prices.
2. Amazon: AWS has years of work lined up
Amazon's cloud business is the top reason I'd hold the stock through 2030. Amazon Web Services (AWS) revenue climbed 39% year over year to $46.0 billion in the third quarter, its fastest growth in almost five years. And AWS brought in about 63% of Amazon's operating income on about 23% of its sales.
What's more, AWS's backlog (contracted revenue it hasn't recognized yet) hit $578 billion. That's over three years of revenue at AWS's current $184 billion annual run rate.
"[W]e believe that AWS can grow north of 40% in each of 2027 and in 2028 and be a trillion-dollar revenue business in the next five to 10 years," CEO Andy Jassy said on Amazon's third-quarter earnings call.
AMZN Amazon
NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/13/26
Of course, growth like this costs a lot. Amazon expects around $220 billion in cash capital expenditures this year, and Jassy said it plans to spend "meaningfully more" in 2027. Free cash flow for the last 12 months was negative $42.4 billion, versus positive $14.8 billion a year before.
3. IBM: AI agents, sold with Microsoft
IBM is the slowest grower of the three. Management expects revenue to climb 4% to 5% at constant currency this year (a measure that removes exchange-rate changes).
But a new product may help where IBM has struggled. On Nov. 10, IBM and Microsoft (MSFT +0.17%) announced Imagine Enterprise, a platform that helps businesses make and manage artificial intelligence (AI) agents for their industries. This article originally appeared in the Spring 2025 issue of Runner’s World.
“What fresh hell is this?” Liz B. wondered during a four-mile run on a chilly December night five months after giving birth. She was 2.7 miles into an out-and-back route when she realized she’d leaked a little urine. “It happened on and off the rest of the way home,” says the 36-year-old from central Ohio, who prefers not to use her full name when talking about urinary incontinence, which affects 25 million adult Americans.
This was not how she had envisioned her postpartum life. Liz, a physical therapist who works with stroke, brain injury, and spinal cord injury patients, had been a runner for nearly her whole life. Her father, who just ran his 91st marathon at the age of 77, had taken her out for jogs when she was a toddler, and she was hooked on long distances ever since. Her idea of a “good time” was waking up at 5 a.m. on a Saturday to go for a scenic 16-mile run with her sister. Before becoming a mom, she’d run eight marathons and was eight minutes shy of qualifying for Boston. “I had always been excited to get pregnant and had dreams of pushing my kid in a running stroller.” But her regular runs came to a screeching halt 19 weeks into her pregnancy when she developed peripheral blood clots and had to reduce physical activity because of the pain. She’d been looking forward to lacing up her running shoes again, but after a difficult labor, she developed pelvic organ prolapse, a condition where weak muscles allow one or more pelvic organs (like the uterus or bladder) to drop down onto other organs or out of the vagina.
Liz had been working with a pelvic floor therapist to treat the prolapse and had just spent the previous six weeks easing back into running. But she was frustrated with the slow progress in coming back to her pre-pregnancy eight-minute mile. “Once I had my baby, my pace slowed to a 10:30 mile,” Liz says. “And if I ran under a 9:00, I’d pee my pants a little.”
Pelvic floor dysfunction, an inability to coordinate pelvic floor muscles, is more prevalent than most of us realize. Research shows that approximately 1 in 3 women and 1 in 6 men will experience pelvic floor dysfunction in their lifetime—and that’s just what gets reported. Particularly in women, hormonal fluctuations, added weight, and the strain of pregnancy and childbirth can weaken the pelvic floor.
As much as we dislike the fact, high-impact physical activity—like running—can exacerbate these issues. That’s because as you run, your pelvic floor repeatedly absorbs impact and dampens vibrations, says Julie W. Wiebe, DPT, a physical therapist in Los Angeles who specializes in returning women to fitness after injury and pregnancy.
“Running creates an added challenge to your pelvic floor beyond the movements of everyday activities,” explains Carrie Pagliano, PT, a pelvic floor specialist based in Arlington, Virginia. “It puts greater impact and pressure on your musculoskeletal system.”
The good news is these issues can be resolved. But too often, they go undiagnosed. For one thing, there’s the stigma. Talking about pelvic floor issues can feel taboo because we’ve been conditioned to have shame around that area of the body. What’s more, most of us aren’t even sure where our pelvic floor is, what it does, or how it can become dysfunctional. His Credit Card May Cover a Broken or Stolen Phone, as Long as He Pays His Phone Bill With It
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
A cracked screen or a stolen phone can lead to a costly repair or a new phone, but some cardholders already have coverage for this through a credit card. Credit card cell phone protection is a card benefit that can pay for a broken or stolen phone, as long as you pay your monthly wireless bill with that card.
A card benefit is a perk the issuer builds into the card at no separate charge, and a deductible is the amount the cardholder pays out of pocket on each claim before the benefit covers the rest.
How Paying the Phone Bill Switches On Coverage
Once the cardholder charges the monthly cell phone bill to an eligible card, the phones on that bill are covered against damage and theft. If something happens, the cardholder files a claim, pays the deductible, and gets reimbursed for a repair or replacement, and each card sets a limit per claim and a cap per year.
One Cellular Telephone Protection guide to benefits, as of 07/01/2021, spells out the schedule. Coverage starts the first day of the calendar month after a wireless bill is paid. If a month’s bill isn’t paid with the card, coverage is suspended until a later bill is paid with it.
What Two Big Issuers Publish Right Now
Limits vary from card to card. Wells Fargo (NYSE:WFC | WFC Price Prediction) lists up to $600 of cell phone protection against damage or theft on its Active Cash card, subject to a $25 deductible. The product page compares benefits as of 04/28/2026, and the card has a $0 annual fee.
Capital One (NYSE:COF) says Venture X cardholders who pay their phone bill with the card can get reimbursed up to $800. The reimbursement applies if the phone is stolen or damaged. Terms, conditions, and exclusions apply. That card has a $395 annual fee.
The older guide lists lower limits than these two cards. It pays $200 per claim, with a maximum of two (2) claims and $400 per twelve (12) month period and a $50 deductible. Issuers update these benefits, so only the current guide for the specific card counts.
Which Phones Qualify and Which Get Left Out
Coverage generally follows the bill that was paid. Under the guide, eligible phones are the lines listed on the most recent wireless statement for the billing period before the event. A family plan paid with the card may cover every line on it. A phone on a separate bill paid some other way doesn’t qualify.
The same guide also excludes rented and borrowed phones, phones on pre-paid or “pay as you go” plans, and phones bought for resale or commercial use.
Requirements for Keeping Coverage Active Before the Next Drop
- The card’s Guide to Benefits lists the terms. Wells Fargo tells cardholders to call the number on the back of the card to request a copy.
- The guide lists the per-claim limit, the yearly cap, the deductible, and the claim deadlines.
- Coverage requires the monthly wireless bill to be paid with that card.
- Copies of wireless statements show the card payment.
- After a theft, the guide requires a police report, filed within forty-eight (48) hours.
- Claims usually rely on repair estimates, receipts, and photos of the damage.
Exclusions That Can Block a Claim
Lost phones are a common gap. The guide excludes phones that are lost or “mysteriously disappear” with no evidence that someone took them.

"This is actually a bigger deal for humanity than most people can imagine," Walter Isaacson, Elon Musk's biographer, wrote on X after SpaceX (NASDAQ: SPCX) caught its Starship spacecraft with the launch tower's arms on Nov. 14. Musk shared the post with a message of his own: "The epic day has arrived, thanks to the incredibly talented team at SpaceX!"
Isaacson also recalled the engineers' reactions in a Starbase conference room in December 2020, when Musk pushed the idea that the tower's arms could catch a returning Starship.
Hours after the catch, Musk reshared his Aug. 30, 2021, post calling the tower arms "robot chopsticks," which warned that "success is not guaranteed, but excitement is!" On Flight 15, he got half of each. The rocket's Super Heavy booster, which was supposed to be caught the same way, was diverted and exploded in the Gulf of Mexico. SpaceX has caught three earlier versions of the booster, the first in October 2024, but this was the first attempt with its newest design.
SpaceX shares closed at $139.11 on Nov. 13, about 3% above the $135 IPO price, then slipped about 2% in after-hours trading as the booster was lost. Nov. 16 is the market's first chance to react to the catch. The next test comes Dec. 8, when the last batch of insider shares from the IPO lockup can be sold.
Ship 42 kept climbing into orbit, which Starship first reached on the previous flight, on Sept. 28. About 35 minutes after liftoff, it began releasing 26 Starlink V3 satellites, a batch SpaceX says adds roughly 10 times the downlink capacity of a Falcon 9 Starlink launch. Three of the satellites carried cameras to photograph the ship's heat shield, which SpaceX checked before committing to bring it home. The ship then circled Earth about 14 times.
Musk and SpaceX engineers were inspecting the ship within hours. "I hugged ship 42 upon its return," he posted, along with videos showing it "looks great!"
The ship's condition matters because SpaceX wants to fly it again. A reusable rocket is supposed to make launches far cheaper, and cheaper launches mean more Starlink satellites. SpaceX told CNN it aims to reliably reuse Starship by NASA's Artemis IV moon mission, slated for 2028, though NASA hasn't decided whether Starship or Blue Origin's Blue Moon will land that crew.
Before the flight, Morgan Stanley analyst Adam Jonas called a successful catch one of the most significant potential catalysts in SpaceX's history.
You may think you own a rocket company
In the third quarter, SpaceX reported revenue of $14.58 billion, up 161% from a year earlier and well above the $12.72 billion analysts expected. Net income was $4.4 billion, helped by about $1 billion of other income and a $390 million tax benefit. Income from operations was $2.8 billion.
Its AI business, which the company calls "Super Intelligence," brought in $7.56 billion, topping the $5.25 billion from Connectivity, the segment that includes Starlink, for the first time. The Space segment, home to Starship, lost $7 million as research spending on the rocket rose.
Starlink had 13.6 million consumer subscribers at Sept. 30. Average monthly revenue per user rose to $69 from $66 in the second quarter but was still below $83 a year earlier. SpaceX is also pushing Starlink into the phone business.
Cheap launches matter to the stock because SpaceX is its own biggest customer. Of the 476 metric tons it put in orbit last quarter, 358 were its own payloads.

It is easy to get excited about big news events, and few things have been bigger lately than politics. Regardless of your political views, tying your investment strategy to a Republican or Democratic success story isn't likely to set you up for long-term investment success. Why? Because the United States holds elections every two years.
In other words, the political winds can change very quickly. And they often do, noting that the big Democratic win in the midterm elections came just two years after a big Republican win during the presidential election. This is why you may want to consider buying companies like Procter & Gamble (PG +1.05%), Federal Realty (FRT +0.35%), and NextEra Energy (NEE -0.20%). Here's a deeper dive into each one and the sector they represent.
Procter & Gamble: You aren't going to stop buying toilet paper
Procter & Gamble is one of the world's largest consumer staples companies. It is a Dividend King, with over 50 annual dividend increases. It offers an attractive and well-above-market 2.6% dividend yield. But the real story here is that it sells products you are going to buy regardless of who occupies the White House or controls the Senate and House. In fact, you'll keep buying the toilet paper, toothpaste, and cough medicines that P&G makes right through bear markets and recessions, too. These products are life necessities.
PG Procter & Gamble
NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/13/26
What makes P&G extra attractive is that it has long focused on leading the industry through innovation. The goal is to make products that customers are willing to pay for, which was on clear display in the first quarter of fiscal 2027. Despite budget tightening among consumers, P&G organic sales rose a healthy 4%. P&G is a very well-run consumer staples business, and even the most conservative investor should feel comfortable owning it for the long term. But the business is a strong representative of a sector whose demand isn't tied to the political cycle.
Location, location, location will always matter
Fedearl Realty is the only Dividend King real estate investment trust (REIT). It uses a sharpshooter approach, owning only about 100 strip-mall and mixed-use properties. Essentially, its properties are located in areas with large populations of wealthy customers. It also invests significant time and money in development and redevelopment to ensure its properties are leading destinations in the regions they serve. Retailers want to be located in Fedeal Realty assets because the locations can't be replicated.
FRT Federal Realty Investment Trust
NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/13/26
The stock's yield is hovering around 4% right now, but the real story here is all about location, location, location. A REIT with a great portfolio of assets isn't watching the political cycle. It focuses on serving its tenants and their customers well because the properties it owns will remain for decades. Two years is a drop in the bucket. Microsoft Corp. said access has been fully restored to its flagship software, ending an outage that paralyzed government offices, traders and businesses around the world.
“All products are operational,” according to a service health status update on its website. A “backlog of email messages has been processed, thus this issue is remediated,” it said of its Microsoft 365 services.
That included Outlook, Teams and the Copilot artificial intelligence tool, whose users experienced missed meeting invitations and unresponsive web pages on Friday. Previous disruptions have rarely lasted more than several hours.
The outage cascaded around the world, with people in more than 70 countries reporting problems, according to Downdetector, which recorded hundreds of thousands of complaints.
Office and government workers from Tokyo to London and New York struggled to adapt, often reaching for analog 20th-century tools like the telephone and, yes, paper. Corporate workers around the US celebrated the Outlook outage as an “adult snow day.” Google Workspace workers, meanwhile, looked on with envy as their Outlook counterparts kicked up their feet.
But their bosses were already counting the costs. Some companies, including Swiss luxury group Richemont and US-based truck and bus manufacturer Workhorse Group Inc., were forced to delay reporting their financial results. Critical services including police departments and hospitals were affected, with the UK’s National Health Service rescheduling some procedures, according to people familiar with the matter.
The failure and the time it took to find a fix was a black eye for Microsoft, whose Windows operating system and productivity apps remain critical infrastructure in the age of artificial intelligence. The company’s M365 software bundle has more than 450 million commercial users. Once again, critics highlighted the risks of entrusting so much power to one provider — even as many people understood that unshackling themselves from Microsoft’s ubiquitous products was unlikely anytime soon. Investors largely shrugged off the incident, with Microsoft shares little changed.
“We do not expect the incident to meaningfully change Microsoft’s competitive position in the near term, given the high cost and complexity of replacing deeply embedded productivity workflows,” William Blair & Co. analyst Jason Ader wrote in a note. “Longer term, however, it could make some customers more receptive to alternatives, particularly Google Workspace and emerging productivity offerings from Anthropic unveiled earlier this week.”
The error was introduced during a network capacity upgrade, a spokesperson said. The company’s response, detailed in hourly updates to the company’s status page, described some false starts as Microsoft struggled to pin down the issue.
More than 1,000 engineers and other employees gathered on video calls led by cloud chief Scott Guthrie and Charles Lamanna, who oversees the M365 bundle and other workplace applications. Sessions ran late Thursday and spilled into Friday morning.
Exchange, the digital backbone powering email and calendars in the M365 bundle, would start up on a server and quickly consume its available resources, leading it to become unresponsive. Engineers investigated whether the application was mistakenly firing traffic at databases rather than local memory, according to a person familiar with the matter. Japan's economy unexpectedly contracted in the third quarter, shrinking at an annualized 0.1% compared to the previous quarter, as elevated energy prices weighed on consumption and net exports.
A Reuters poll of economists had estimated the economy to grow at 0.3% in the three months to September, while GDP had expanded at 1.4% in the previous quarter.
Japan's exports beat expectations for two of the three months in the quarter, but net exports weighed on the economy due to higher costs of energy imports, cutting 0.6 percentage point from the country's growth.
Energy subsidies for households had reportedly expired in September, exposing consumers to higher energy prices brought about by the Iran war.

Has Microsoft Stock Become A Different Bet?
For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.
Microsoft (MSFT) stock trades at 27.3 times earnings, against 21.9 for the S&P 500. At that price you want to know exactly what you own, and the company’s priorities have moved. During its fiscal Q2 2025 call in January 2025, management talked up customers such as UBS moving workloads to Azure, and it still made the case for cloud migrations a year later. On its October 2026 call, management emphasized something else. What does management talk up now instead?
Microsoft Now Talks Up Foundry And AI Agents
Management now emphasizes Foundry, the platform customers use to build AI agents and deploy them at scale, calling it an increasingly important driver of growth. On the October 28, 2026 call, management said Azure revenue grew 48% in fiscal Q1 2027, driven by Foundry and by earning more from its CPU capacity.
A cloud migration moves a customer’s existing work onto Azure, Microsoft’s cloud. On the fiscal Q4 2025 call in July 2025, management said Azure had passed $75 billion in annual revenue, up 34%.
Investors paying a premium for Microsoft appear to be betting that Azure can keep growing on new AI work rather than on workloads moved over from elsewhere. So far management has named Foundry as a driver of Azure’s growth in fiscal Q1 2027, though it said that growth also spanned core cloud services.
How Big Are Azure And Foundry Now?
Management said on the July 29, 2026 call that Azure passed $100 billion in revenue in fiscal 2026, up 41%. Microsoft’s total revenue passed $331 billion that year, up 18%, so Azure grew more than twice as fast as the company.
That gap held in the latest quarter. Microsoft’s revenue rose 18.8% in fiscal Q1 2027, well short of Azure’s pace.
Foundry is growing faster still. Microsoft now has more than 120,000 Foundry customers, and management said Foundry revenue more than tripled from a year earlier. Foundry feeds a cloud business already worth more than $100 billion a year.
Is Microsoft’s New Focus Reassuring For Holders?
On growth, the shift looks reassuring. You also want to know what the data centers behind that growth cost. In fiscal Q1 2027, Microsoft’s cash from operations rose to $58.0 billion from $45.1 billion a year earlier. Yet as reported, fiscal Q1 2027 free cash flow, the cash left after capital spending, fell to $18.6 billion from $25.7 billion a year earlier.
Management expects capital expenditures of more than $50 billion in fiscal Q2 2027, against $45.2 billion in fiscal Q1. That measure counts finance leases in full when each lease starts. The cash Microsoft paid for property, plant and equipment in Q1 was $39.4 billion. Management’s guide for the full fiscal 2027 is that Microsoft will remain free cash flow positive, and management said it will tap additional sources of funding when it finds them attractive. At the end of September 2026, Microsoft held $64.3 billion of cash and short-term investments, more than its $57.2 billion of debt.
So Foundry is one named driver of Azure’s growth so far, while the cash that pays for the data centers is the weaker side. If free cash flow falls further, holders own a faster-growing Microsoft that keeps less of its sales as cash. Azure growth, against management’s guide of 49% to 50% in constant currency for fiscal Q2 2027, and free cash flow are the two numbers to watch when Microsoft reports in January 2027.

Adobe’s Sam Garfield: AI has Sped Up Creative, But Organizations Haven’t Kept Pace
RANCHO PALOS VERDES, CALIF. — Creative ideation that once took weeks now takes days, and sometimes hours. Versioning an asset across channels, formats, and aspect ratios has sped up just as much. The slowdown has moved somewhere else.
According to Sam Garfield, head of Digital Strategy, CMT, Data and AI Platforms at Adobe, the friction now sits inside the enterprise operating model. AI works well within individual functions, and companies struggle to roll it out across workflows.
“58% of the companies we talk to are in what we call the frozen middle,” Garfield told Beet.TV contributor David Kaplan at Beet Retreat LA, citing Adobe’s research on organizational readiness. “That means they’re stuck in their AI deployment, either in a pilot or not being able to deploy at scale.”
Moving to the left
Garfield describes the creative process as a content supply chain, and AI is changing how it starts. A creative brief used to be a document. Now it can kick off the generation of creative and the pulling of an audience in a single automated workflow.
One Adobe customer summed up the goal for her team in a phrase Garfield liked. She wanted them to “move to the left,” toward strategy at the start of the process and away from production at the end.
“What we’re doing is helping teams move to the left,” Garfield said.
One-stop agencies
Asked whether agency value is shifting toward strategy, audience insight, data stewardship, or orchestration, Garfield answered “all of the above.” Agencies are collapsing the silos that once separated creative, media, and activation, and clients increasingly expect a single integrated offering. Adobe, he said, is the operating system many agencies are building on top of.
Data that doesn’t connect
Audience data exists, and so does creative effectiveness data. Garfield sees the challenge in joining the two. A Winterberry Group study Garfield mentioned found that every company surveyed is measuring creative effectiveness or planning to, but only 6% use it at every point in the process.
“The data exists, but connecting the data and making sure that’s flowing back into which audience you select and then through the creative for effectiveness measurement is not happening at scale,” Garfield said.
Governance by design
Garfield argues that brand safety and rights compliance can’t be a gate at the end of the process when AI moves this quickly. Adobe has built those capabilities into its products, including brand intelligence checks such as whether a generated asset places the logo correctly.
“We don’t look at governance as something that happens at the end, as sort of a gate at the end. It has to be designed as part of the feature set,” Garfield said.

Masco NYSE: MAS expects to grow in 2026 despite challenging conditions in its product categories, but it is not counting on a major market recovery in 2027, President and CEO Jon Nudi said at Baird’s Global Industrial Conference.
Nudi said the home improvement and building products company expects low-single-digit growth in 2026 while maintaining strong profit margins. Masco has set a target of 3% to 4% organic growth through 2028, a goal that assumes some return to category growth.
“As we look to 2027, we are not assuming a major inflection,” Nudi said. “We feel like we have got to make our own way, both from a top line and a bottom line standpoint.”
Growth and cost priorities
Nudi said Masco is seeking to outgrow its product categories while preserving its focus on margins and operational discipline. The company, which he described as having just under $8 billion in revenue and margins in the high teens, is investing in innovation and digital capabilities while working to reduce costs.
Masco announced a $50 million restructuring at the end of the fourth quarter of last year, Nudi said. He added that the company would remain aggressive in adjusting its cost structure to the size of its markets and business.
The company has also integrated its Newport Brass and Liberty Hardware businesses into Delta Faucet. Nudi said the moves let the smaller businesses draw on Delta’s customer relationships and e-commerce capabilities, while producing cost synergies. He said the businesses are seeing higher revenue as a result.
Masco has focused on repair and remodeling rather than new construction, Nudi said. Replacement purchases for broken products have remained robust, and smaller remodeling projects have held up fairly well, while larger remodels have slowed.
He said the company would provide 2027 guidance when it reports earnings in February. Some inflation is likely next year, he said, but Masco works with suppliers and removes costs from its own operations before raising prices.
Plumbing and wellness opportunities
In plumbing, Nudi said Masco is focused on winning business across wholesale, retail and e-commerce. The company is gaining shelf space at most big-box retailers this year, he said, while e-commerce is among its fastest-growing businesses. Masco sells almost nothing directly to consumers, instead using channels such as Home Depot’s website, Ferguson Home and Amazon.
Nudi said the company is also adapting its digital strategy as consumers increasingly use artificial intelligence tools to research products. Masco is working to ensure its brands appear as intended in searches using large language models, which draw on sources including websites, long-form content and online discussions.
Higher-end plumbing brands Brizo and Newport Brass have shown momentum as upper-income consumers continue to spend, Nudi said. Masco is preparing to open a Brizo and Newport Brass showroom in New York City in the first quarter of 2027, aimed at designers and architects who specify products for projects.

An evacuation order that forced hundreds of people from their homes near an industrial site in central Illinois was lifted Saturday after law enforcement agencies completed a search of the area, authorities said.
A bomb was discovered Friday afternoon at the BioUrja Renewables facility in Peoria. Police said the device had been “rendered safe,” but authorities ordered residents within a 1-mile radius to evacuate while the surrounding area was searched.
State, federal and local law enforcement conducted an extensive search at the facility and “they have found no other items of concern,” the Peoria Police Department said on its Facebook account on Saturday. “Residents are now free to return to their homes in the area that was affected,” the police said, adding that all roads will be opened and the investigation will continue.
FBI Special Agent Ryan Presley said his agency was investigating, but declined to provide further details.
“We will work tirelessly to identify the individual responsible and bring them to justice,” he said.
No arrests have been made at this time, and no injuries have been reported.
Peoria Mayor Rita Ali told WMBD-TV on Friday that BioUrja is “a plant that has ethanol and highly combustible types of chemicals, and so that’s what alarms us.”
It is not unusual for law enforcement to receive bomb threats and suspicious package calls, but they often don’t result in a credible threat, even though such calls are taken seriously by officials who must assess and investigate the claims.
Just earlier this week, hundreds of airline passengers in Europe had their flights diverted or given military escorts after a series of bomb threats that officials have since declared were malicious hoaxes.
“We understand that this is a disruptive process for our residents and guests,” Peoria Police Chief Brad Dixon said. “We’re asking for the public’s patience while we work to make this area safe.”
Peoria, with a population of around 110,000, is located about 150 miles (about 240 kilometers) southwest of Chicago.
The BioUrja plant is located along the Illinois River. The company acquired the ethanol plant in 2021.

The Florida Surplus Lines Service Office announced a $12 million gift to Florida State University’s risk management and insurance program, a grant that should enable deeper research into Florida’s ever-evolving insurance landscape.
It’s by far the largest grant yet for FSLSO, which has donated $2.5 million to universities in the state since the stamping office began operations 28 years ago.
The endowment, which leaders with FSU’s Herbert Wertheim College of Business called “transformational,” reflects the growing presence of excess and surplus lines coverage in Florida, a state that in recent years saw many policyholders turn to surplus lines because of rising primary-market premiums and insurers’ litigation costs.
Surplus lines’ policy counts in Florida climbed from less than 1.2 million in 2020, for example, to more than 1.7 million in 2025. Total surplus lines’ premium in the state more than doubled, from $7.5 billion in 2020 to $17.3 billion in 2025, the FSLSO’s annual reports indicate.
The Surplus Lines Office, established by Florida statute in 1997, is a non-profit, quasi-governmental body that oversees compliance and collection of taxes on surplus lines policies, as well as an online portal for insurance agents and some back-office support for seven other states’ stamping offices.
The FSLSO appears to be well positioned to provide large grants: Last year, the organization reported almost $20 million in revenue from stamping fees and assessments on surplus policies. That’s more than double its revenue in 2020 and well above its reported 2025 expenses of $11.5 million. Total assets stood at almost $78 million, the annual report shows.
If anyone should question whether such revenue and margins are appropriate, the FSLSO’s director of communications pointed out that the office this year slashed its stamping fee in half, bringing it from .06% per policy to .03%. That’s less than $300 per policy and is the lowest among surplus lines stamping offices nationwide, FSLSO Communications Director Ashlee Weber noted.
The average surplus lines premium was about $7,700 in the third quarter of this year, the Office reported.
The $12 million endowment to FSU will establish the Florida Surplus Lines Center for Insurance Excellence and will be used to fund faculty salary stipends, student assistance, conferences and more.
“Our continued support, including this endowment, reflects our commitment to strengthening both the surplus lines industry and the broader insurance marketplace by investing in the education, research and talent that will shape the future,” Mark Shealy, FSLSO’s executive director, said in a statement.
Shealy graduated from FSU with a bachelor’s degree in accounting in 1991 before starting his career in the insurance industry.
The center will be led by FSU Professor Charles Nyce, who is already known for his department’s research into property-casualty insurance in recent years. Nyce’s position as director was funded by a separate, $1 million grant from the FSLSO that was announced in August.
Nyce said the center will be able to delve deeply into many areas of insurance, including property, liability and health insurance.

When Jane Kim claimed victory in the race for California insurance commissioner over fellow Democrat Ben Allen less than a week after the Nov. 3 election, the insurance industry may have gotten a more progressive and pro-consumer advocate than it has had in years.
Kim is a more progressive candidate than Allen, who was focused on making insurance affordable and fighting climate change in his work in the state Legislature.
Kim, an attorney and consumer advocate, served on San Francisco’s Board of Supervisors from 2011 to 2019. She has also run for state Senate and for San Francisco mayor. Her platform included providing natural disaster insurance for everyone, ensuring that premiums go to paying for claims, increasing transparency from insurers and investing in safer homes and communities.
U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), for whom she served as California political director, the California Teachers Association and the Working Families Party all endorsed Kim.
Kim had 54.2% of the vote with all precincts reporting at least partially in. Vote-by-mail ballots, provisional ballots and other ballots are being tallied, but her lead has continued to grow to more than 900,000 votes over Allen.
She will replace outgoing commissioner Ricardo Lara, who is term limited.
Kim is also proposing a public program to cover wildfire risk for existing homes in California. In an October outline, she said participation would be mandatory, with premiums based partly on each home’s wildfire risk and partly on rebuilding costs to fund catastrophic losses. Private insurers would continue selling other homeowners coverages, and the public program would invest reserves in wildfire mitigation. The proposal would require support from state lawmakers and the governor.
Affordability was a recurring theme during her campaign, a message Democrats and progressives like her across the country rode to success in the elections.
“We’ve been traveling up and down the state all year and I just believe that our message centered around affordability and fighting to make sure that insurance is there for 40 million Americans in California resonated,” Kim said.
Affordability is what voters have been asking for “over the last decade, but I think that has become particularly untenable the last few years under the Trump Administration,” she added.
Kim is in the process of putting together a transition committee, which she said will include policy experts in insurance, climate and technology leaders throughout the state to discuss plans for her first 100 days in office and what they believe she can accomplish in her first year.
“Our mandate is to make insurance affordable, available and fair, and that is what I will be fighting to do every single day that I’m in office,” Kim said.
One of Lara’s signature efforts over the past few years in office was to work with insurers to get them to return to writing homeowners insurance in the state. US flight disruptions stretched into Sunday as airlines worked to return to normal operations following the four-hour nationwide stoppage on Friday as authorities continued to investigate what caused it.
After canceling more than 6,600 flights on Saturday, airlines scrapped nearly 2,000 on Sunday, with more than 8,600 others being delayed, as of 7 p.m. New York time, according to data from tracker FlightAware.
American Airlines Group Inc. is showing the most canceled flights so far on Sunday, with 630, while JetBlue Airways Corp. has shed more than a quarter of its schedule.
FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said that airlines expect to return to their normal flight schedules by the end of business on Sunday, while he apologized for the disruptive shutdown.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the issue was traced to the replacement of outdated copper wire at a remote location near El Dorado, Arkansas, by L3Harris Technologies Inc., and that a router there started flooding the air-traffic control system with connection attempts.
That router is now undergoing testing at an L3Harris facility, Duffy said, adding that it was still unclear whether the issue was caused by the contractor’s “incompetence” or by a faulty router.
“Those routers were purchased in 2001,” Duffy said on ABC’s This Week. “They were obsolete in 2006, and we still use them in 2026 just to underscore how old the network is.”
The FAA said it is also examining equipment at a site in Amarillo, Texas, that may have also contributed to the overloads. The outage, which began at 3:30 p.m. New York time on Friday, led to instability at 17 of the 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers and spread to several Terminal Radar Approach Controls, the agency said. The shutdown was lifted at 8:15 p.m. on Friday. More than 12,000 flights in total were canceled.
Duffy said the government has looked at the risks that come with upgrading the FAA’s systems and there was no specific suggestion that the work on Friday would lead to a breakdown.
“It’s worked thousands of times when we made the switchover,” Duffy said on CBS’s Face the Nation. “This time it didn’t.”
Duffy focused his criticism on L3Harris.

A cargo ship struck a bridge across the Delaware River on Thursday, disrupting traffic between Palmyra, New Jersey, and Philadelphia, according to a Pennsylvania lawmaker.
The collision left the 3,659-foot-long (1,115-meter-long) Tacony-Palmyra Bridge unable to close, causing a major backup on the Philadelphia side, state Rep. Ed Neilson said in a news release. No injuries have been reported, he said.
The U.S. Coast Guard said the cargo vessel is currently moored at a Kinder Morgan facility in Bristol, Pennsylvania, where an inspection team is on site. The Coast Guard identified the vessel as the 591-foot (180-meter) Strategic Alliance, which was built in 2013 and sails under the flag of Singapore.
The drawbridge was open for ships to pass through at the time of the collision around 1:15 p.m., according to the Coast Guard. It remained open afterward because another vessel needed to pass through, and has since come back down. The bridge reopened to traffic with a lane closure Thursday evening, the Burlington County (New Jersey) Bridge Commission Police Department said.
The steel bridge carries vehicles along Route 73 between Palmyra and the Tacony neighborhood in northeast Philadelphia. It has three lanes of vehicular traffic, two into Philadelphia and one into New Jersey. Estimates from 2025 show the bridge can carry as many as 76,200 vehicles each day.
Opened in 1929, the Tacony-Palmyra toll bridge was found to be in “fair” condition, according to the Federal Highway Administration’s 2026 National Bridge Inventory data released this fall.
Inspectors rated the deck of the Tacony-Palmyra Bridge as in good condition, the substructure as in fair condition and the superstructure — the component that absorbs the live traffic load — as fair.
Associated Press journalists Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City, Julie Carr Smyth in Columbus, Ohio, and Christopher L. Keller in Albuquerque, New Mexico, contributed.

The U.S. Transportation Department wrongly decided to withhold nearly $74 million in highway money from New York state after it refused to revoke nearly 33,000 questionable commercial driver’s licenses for immigrants when an audit revealed problems last year, a federal appeals court said Friday.
A three-judge panel of the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Manhattan concluded in a written decision that the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration, an arm of the Transportation Department, acted in a manner that was “arbitrary, capricious, or contrary to law” when it penalized New York.
The appeals court said the state can’t be faulted for failing to cancel licenses when a commercial driver lost legal status to stay in the United States because rules that would require a cancellation were not in place at the time.
The licenses pertain to commercial vehicles such as trucks, trailers, limousines and buses.
New York Attorney General Letitia James complained when the lawsuit was filed in April that the federal government was unfairly holding back money the state needs to repair roads and bridges. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul in the spring called the federal cuts “devastating” and characterized them as “political payback.”
The Transportation Department said in a statement Friday that it makes no sense for states to let trucking licenses for foreign drivers stretch years beyond when they are legally in the U.S.
“We’ve put a stop to the madness to keep the driving public safe,” the statement said.
Hochul and James welcomed the ruling in a joint statement, calling it “a win for the millions of New Yorkers who rely on safe roads to travel” and for the “drivers who power our state’s economy.”
The Transportation Department began enforcing existing English language requirements for truckers in the summer of 2025. Concerns about truck driver qualifications took on more urgency after an August 2025 crash in Florida, when a truck driver was accused of performing an illegal U-turn that killed three people. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that driver, who is from India, should never have been licensed in the first place.
Audits conducted in every state uncovered numerous non-domiciled commercial driver’s licenses that remained valid long after an immigrant’s work permits had expired or were issued without properly verifying citizenship status.
Since then, about 26,000 drivers have been pulled off the road for failing to demonstrate English proficiency, and the Transportation Department said 30,000 commercial licenses were canceled because they were issued illegally.
Immigrants account for about 20% of all truck drivers while the non-domiciled licenses immigrants can receive represent about 5% of all commercial driver’s licenses or about 200,000 drivers.
Immigrant groups have said they believe that many drivers are being unfairly targeted.
The dispute came after Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy tightened rules governing when immigrants can obtain a commercial driver’s license.
Officials said they took action against states like New York after learning that some licenses remained valid long after an immigrant was no longer authorized to be in the country. New York issued licenses valid for eight years regardless of how long a driver’s visa remained valid, authorities said.
AP Transportation Writer Josh Funk reported from Omaha, Nebraska.

The California Department of Insurance is seeking information from insurers on their use of artificial intelligence as well as public input on potential safeguards covering transparency, accountability, privacy and fairness.
The CDI announced its Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence Survey to examine how insurers are deploying AI technologies, the governance structures used to oversee those systems, the role of third-party vendors and operational impacts associated with AI adoption.
The department is also holding a virtual public workshop Dec. 15 beginning. Consumers, insurance companies, researchers, technology developers, academics, consumer advocates and other interested parties are invited to participate in the 10 a.m. workshop, which will focus on transparency, fairness, privacy, human oversight, accountability and insurer responsibility for technologies supplied by third-party vendors.
Information gathered through the survey and workshop will help the department determine whether additional consumer safeguards, transparency standards or regulatory guidance are needed, according to a CDI announcement about the survey and workshop.
The department plans to use the information collected to inform its AI oversight. Survey responses are due Dec. 30.
